newsitem.title: USA: Continental, Delta deal could spark consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Continental, Delta deal could spark consolidation.

text.p: A possible merger between Continental Airlines Inc and Delta Air Lines Inc would force an industry-wide consolidation that would increase air fares and limit customer choice, industry experts said.
A merger of the two airlines, valued at an estimated $2 billion, would create the nation's largest airline. Both Delta and Continental declined to comment on rumors of merger talks.

"It's kind of like going to a dance. Once someone makes a move to ask someone to dance, everyone else scrambles for a partner," said Richard Gritta, a University of Portland professor of business specializing in the airline industry.
Industry experts said that an airline industry consolidation would push up fares over the long-term and limit consumer choice.
"It will encourage mega-mergers among the major carriers, creating an oligarchy," Gritta said.
"The (airline) industry is in a mature phase and consolidation is the final phase of that maturation process," said Brian Harris, an airline analyst with Lehman Brothers.
Harris said a possible Continental-Delta deal is a "a very sound strategic fit, with a lot of good synergies."

The proposed deal would be an "easier combination" than a link between USAir Group Inc and UAL Corp's United Airlines, since Delta and Continental have more compatible fleets and less unionization, Harris said.
USAir put itself up for sale last year and held talks with United and AMR Corp's American Airlines. Those talks were later called off.
USAir continues to top analysts' lists of potential acquisition targets. Despite that speculation, USAir reiterated Wednesday its desire to remain independent.
"Our sole focus is on internally generated growth," said USAir spokesman Rick Weintraub.
USAir's stock gained 1-1/8 to 25-1/2 on Wednesday.
Airlines are now better positioned to pursue acquisitions than in the past, industry experts said.
Despite increasing fuel costs, U.S. carriers have posted record earnings in 1996 after losing $13 billion in the first half of the decade.
Analysts expect the airlines to seek partners of similar size with complementary routes, instead of looking to acquire small, regional airlines.
Regional carriers such as ValuJet Inc and Southwest Airlines Co have forced major airlines such as USAir and Delta into defensive positions in certain markets.
But it is unlikely that the major carriers would see more than piecemeal market share gains by absorbing regional carriers, analysts said.
"Small start-up carriers are not nearly as compatible or attractive as they were in the past," said Mark Shields, a vice president in the aviation practice at Mercer Management Consulting.
Shields expects any future combinations among airlines "with longer histories which have a more pervasive market presence."
Despite the long-term pressure on airlines to consolidate routes and cut costs, Shields cautions that one deal may not spark a merger frenzy.
"A single merger may not open the flood gates," Shields said. "Consolidation in the future will follow an eccentric pattern."
